description: Medical tests and diagnostic procedures for menopause

entries.title: Clinical Diagnosis
entries.description: Diagnosing menopause based on symptoms and menstrual history
entries.content: Menopause is typically diagnosed clinically based on symptoms and menstrual history, without the need for blood tests. If you're over 45 and experiencing typical menopausal symptoms with irregular or absent periods, a healthcare provider can usually diagnose perimenopause or menopause without testing. Menopause is confirmed when you've gone 12 consecutive months without a period.
entries.when_used: Primary method of diagnosis for most women over 45
what_provider_considers: Typical symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, etc.)
advantages: No testing needed in most cases
Symptoms and menstrual history are usually sufficient
entries.when_to_see_doctor: If you're experiencing symptoms and want to discuss diagnosis and treatment options

entries.title: FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) Test
entries.description: Blood test measuring FSH levels to assess menopausal status
entries.content: FSH is a hormone that rises as the ovaries produce less estrogen. A blood test measuring FSH levels can suggest whether you're in perimenopause or menopause. However, because hormone levels fluctuate significantly during perimenopause, FSH tests are not always reliable for diagnosis and are not routinely recommended. They may be used in specific situations, such as premature menopause or when diagnosis is unclear.
entries.interpretation: High FSH levels suggest menopause, but levels fluctuate during perimenopause
when_used: When using hormonal contraception that masks symptoms
limitations: Hormone levels fluctuate during perimenopause, so results can be inconsistent
A single test may not be accurate
Not needed for most women over 45 with typical symptoms
entries.home_tests: Home FSH urine tests are available but have same limitations; not recommended for diagnosis
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Discuss if you're under 45 with symptoms or diagnosis is unclear

entries.title: Estradiol Test
entries.content: Estradiol is the main form of estrogen produced by the ovaries. Levels decline during menopause. A blood test can measure estradiol levels, but like FSH, levels fluctuate during perimenopause, making single tests unreliable. This test is not routinely needed for diagnosis but may be used in specific situations.
entries.interpretation: Low estradiol suggests menopause, but levels fluctuate during perimenopause
entries.limitations: Levels fluctuate during perimenopause; not routinely needed
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Discuss if recommended by your healthcare provider

entries.title: TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone) Test
entries.description: Blood test to rule out thyroid problems that can mimic menopause
entries.content: Thyroid problems, particularly hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid), can cause symptoms very similar to menopause, including fatigue, weight gain, mood changes, irregular periods, brain fog, and temperature regulation issues. A TSH blood test checks thyroid function and is often recommended to rule out thyroid disease when evaluating menopausal symptoms, especially if symptoms are atypical or severe.
entries.what_it_measures: Thyroid-stimulating hormone to assess thyroid function
entries.why_important: Thyroid problems can mimic menopause symptoms and need different treatment
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Often checked as part of menopause evaluation, especially with family history of thyroid disease

entries.title: Bone Density Test (DEXA Scan)
entries.description: Scan to measure bone strength and assess osteoporosis risk
entries.content: A bone density test, also called DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scan or bone densitometry, measures bone mineral density to assess bone strength and osteoporosis risk. It's recommended for postmenopausal women to screen for osteoporosis, as estrogen decline after menopause significantly increases bone loss and fracture risk.
entries.what_it_measures: Bone mineral density, typically in spine and hips
when_recommended: Postmenopausal women under 65 with risk factors
entries.procedure: Quick, painless scan using low-dose X-rays
entries.interpretation: Results show bone density compared to healthy young adults (T-score)
entries.why_important: Identifies osteoporosis early so treatment can prevent fractures
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Discuss screening recommendations based on your age and risk factors

entries.title: Pelvic Ultrasound and Biopsy
entries.description: Imaging and tissue sampling to investigate abnormal bleeding
entries.content: If you have abnormal bleeding patterns, especially bleeding after menopause, your doctor may order a pelvic ultrasound to examine the uterus and ovaries, and possibly an endometrial biopsy to sample the uterine lining. This is crucial to rule out serious conditions like uterine cancer, which can cause post-menopausal bleeding.
procedures: Transvaginal ultrasound: Imaging to view uterus and ovaries
Endometrial biopsy: Small tissue sample from uterine lining
entries.why_important: Post-menopausal bleeding can be a sign of uterine cancer and must be investigated
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Immediately for any bleeding after menopause or very heavy/prolonged bleeding
